bibliographic.title: Learning a Markov reward function for evaluating soccer decision making

scope.rationale: Paper learns a Markov Decision Process model of soccer from event stream data to evaluate in-game decision making, including rating players' decision-making riskiness and analyzing shooting policies.

model.name: Markov model for soccer decision making (Van Roy et al. 2021)
inputs: on-the-ball action type (pass, cross, dribble, shoot)
body part used to execute the pass
start and end locations of the previous three actions in the sequence
xG values of shots (used in counterfactual policy use case)
model.target: Per-state value V_pi(s) = probability of eventually scoring from state s under the team's policy; intermediate models predict P(action success) per state-action and pi(a|s) per state.
model.architecture: Hierarchical Bayesian model (Bernoulli/Categorical with Normal log-odds and Half-Normal variances, weakly-informative priors via Gaussian-smoothed counts) fit with PyMC3 ADVI; XGBoost gradient boosted trees ensembles for predicting intended end locations of failed passes and crosses; domain-knowledge post-processing; Bellman value iteration / fundamental matrix for derived quantities; PRISM probabilistic model checking for policy queries.
model.spatial_resolution: Two grids: (a) offensive grid with defensive half as one state and offensive half split into 3m x 3m zones; (b) regular grid of 12 x 16 cells
model.temporal_horizon: until end of possession (absorbing states: lost_possession, no_goal, goal)

metrics: mean absolute error vs. empirically derived state values
baselines: Baseline predicting prior distribution over observed end locations (for end-location prediction)
Non-hierarchical (unpooled) Bayesian model with zero-mean Normal prior (sd=5.0) per team (for transition/policy models)
evaluation.splits: 70-30 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation for XGBoost hyperparameter tuning on successful passes/crosses; Bayesian models evaluated using PSIS-LOO-CV; complete Markov model validated by comparing model-derived state values to empirically computed state values from raw data. Splits are event-level for end-location prediction (not match-level).

claims.statement: With domain-knowledge post-processing, the pass intended-end-location model achieves AUROC 0.99 (+/- 0.00) and Brier 0.54 (+/- 0.02) on the offensive grid, and AUROC 0.99 (+/- 0.00) and Brier 0.69 (+/- 0.03) on the full regular grid, outperforming the XGBoost-only and prior-distribution baselines.

With domain-knowledge post-processing, the cross intended-end-location model achieves AUROC 0.95 (+/- 0.01) / Brier 0.77 (+/- 0.06) on the offensive grid and AUROC 0.95 (+/- 0.02) / Brier 0.58 (+/- 0.08) on the full regular grid.

Hierarchical Bayesian models outperform non-hierarchical (unpooled) versions on PSIS-LOO-CV expected log pointwise predictive density for both policy and transition probability models and for both state spaces (e.g., policy on offensive grid: -167.6 +/- 0.79 hierarchical vs -182.7 +/- 0.80 unpooled).

Mean absolute error between model-derived state values and empirically computed state values, averaged over the six teams, is 0.029 (+/- 0.01) using the offensive grid and 0.018 (+/- 0.01) using the full regular grid.

Counterfactual policy analysis indicates that shooting 20% more often from the identified good long-distance locations would add an estimated 2.5 additional goals per season for Chelsea, 1.6 for Huddersfield/Man City/Man Utd, 1.2 for Newcastle, and 0.7 for Burnley.

All players evaluated received a negative net risk rating, meaning all players perform more conservative actions than risky ones; least-risky top-10 is dominated by Manchester City players (e.g., Zinchenko -50.107), while most-risky top-10 is dominated by Burnley and Newcastle players (e.g., Jacob Murphy -7.697).

Team-specific good shooting locations exist outside the penalty box where shooting immediately yields higher chances of scoring than moving once prior to shooting; locations lie on both sides of the penalty arc for Chelsea, more on the left for Huddersfield, and more centrally for Manchester City.

limitations: Event stream data does not record the intended end location of failed actions, requiring predictive modeling and domain-knowledge post-processing to estimate them.
Data is sparse, particularly near the opponent's goal, motivating the hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage toward a global prior.
No ground truth model is available, making validation of the learned Markov model difficult; the authors must resort to indirect evaluation strategies.
Counterfactual policy changes cannot be implemented in real matches solely for evaluation purposes.
Event stream data contains no information about the location of off-the-ball players, limiting the amount of context that can be included in the model.
